001 Distributed Splunk & multi-source log onboarding One deployment, five log families, validated end to end — then dashboards and alerts someone would actually act on. SIEMSplunkVerified record

Stood up Splunk Enterprise as a distributed deployment — a Deployment Server pushing config to universal forwarders across mixed hosts — then brought several log families into one searchable surface: Windows Event Log, Sysmon, Linux syslog, web application logs and firewall/syslog feeds.

The work that mattered was after ingestion: confirming events actually arrived, fixing field extraction where sourcetypes mis-parsed, normalising time, and turning the result into dashboards and alerts someone would actually act on.

  1. Collect
  2. Parse
  3. Normalise
  4. Validate
Stack
Splunk Enterprise, Deployment Server, Universal Forwarders, SPL
Sources
Windows Event, Sysmon, Linux, web app, firewall
Output
Dashboards, reports, alerts, POC documentation

What it demonstrates Detection is downstream of data quality. The onboarding work — sourcetypes, extraction, time — is what decides whether the alert fires on the right thing.

003 Authorised web application assessment — and the fixes Reproduced, root-caused and remediated three vulnerabilities in a production PHP CMS — including one the original report missed. AppSecWebVerified record

I was interning on the network side, not in security. When an external bug hunter reported two serious flaws in an internal admin panel, I asked the company for permission to work on it, got approval, and only then started testing.

The first two were a SQL injection that bypassed admin login outright, and an HTTP verb tampering flaw that escalated privileges — the authorisation check was written against GET while the application read its parameters from $_REQUEST, so changing the request method walked straight past it. The third I found myself: the dashboard echoed the raw username back into the page instead of reading it from the database, which turned a logic mistake into a reflected XSS vector.

I also worked out that a far smaller payload than the original report used was enough to get in, and documented why — the login logic depended entirely on what the user typed, with nothing behind it.

  1. Reproduce
  2. Root cause
  3. Fix
  4. Re-test
Found
SQL injection (auth bypass) · HTTP verb tampering (privilege escalation) · reflected XSS
Fixed
Input sanitisation, removal of legacy default-password logic, explicit role checks, output encoding, method-pinned parameters, .htaccess hardening
Verified
Re-tested after deploying to production — 3 of 4 items closed, the remainder documented rather than dropped
Rule
Written authorisation before testing, sanitised before publishing

What it demonstrates That I can read the code that caused the flaw, not just run the tool that found it — and that I know to ask permission first.

004 This site — a terminal you can actually use No framework, no build step. A working virtual filesystem, tab completion, and a portrait drawn from 2,473 live glyph particles. Front endCanvasShipped

The page you are reading is itself the case study. There is no framework and no build step — it is plain HTML, one stylesheet, and hand-written JavaScript, which means it loads fast and there is nothing between you and the source.

The shell in the hero is real: a virtual filesystem with ls, cd, cat and tree, fish-style ghost completion on Tab, command history, and a fullscreen mode on Ctrl+K. The portrait above the fold is 2,473 individual glyphs on a canvas — hover it and they are pushed aside and spring back to their exact home position.

The portrait was built the way a halftone is: the source artwork is decomposed into a grid of cells, each cell gets one glyph chosen by how much ink it covers, and the ink colour stays constant — so all the tone comes from density. A single-ink density field reads as text; a per-cell colour palette reads as a washed-out photo. Getting that wrong was the whole difference.

  1. Decompose
  2. Map
  3. Render
  4. Animate
Stack
Vanilla HTML, CSS and JavaScript — no framework, no bundler
Engine
Canvas 2D glyph field, positional particle model, fixed backing store
Detail
JSON-LD, OG/Twitter cards, manifest, self-hosted subset fonts, full no-JS fallback
Verify
View source — every line of it is right there

What it demonstrates Craft under constraint. Accessibility, no-JS resilience and performance were treated as requirements, not clean-up work.
